newsitem.title: USA: Census officials argue merits of sampling in 2000.
newsitem.headline: Census officials argue merits of sampling in 2000.

text.p: The Census Bureau sought to convince skeptical Republicans in Congress Monday that the count of the U.S. population in 2000 will be more accurate if controversial sampling techiques are used.
Republicans have adamantly opposed switching the decennial census away from a strict head-by-head count of each household even though scientific sampling is expected to produce a more accurate count.

Census takers will still go door-to-door, but to supplement this direct count and the mailed questionnaires, the Commerce Department's Census Bureau will use scientific statistical sampling to count those who are normally missed.
In the 1990 census an estimated four million people, over half of them children, were not counted.

"Census 2000 must seek to count everyone, not just those who are easy to find. It is clear that there is only one way to get the most accurate count of the country's population and that is through the limited use of scientific sampling," Census Bureau Director Martha Riche said at a news conference.
The Census Bureau made its arguments for the new technique in a detailed report on the methods it will use to conduct the census. The report was requested by Congress last month.
Acting Undersecretary of Commerce Lee Price told reporters he was confident Congress would see that the new method would reach the goal of the most accurate count possible.

Republicans sought to block funding for the Census Bureau's test of sampling next April when Congress passed the disaster aid bill in June. However, President Clinton threatened to veto the bill if it constrained the Census Bureau.

Republican Rep. Chris Shays of Connecticut, a supporter of sampling, said he felt it would benefit both poor rural and poor urban areas, where the largest numbers of people have been missed in the past.
The census is used to determine the number of congressional districts in each state and to determine a region's share in federal funding for education, food for the poor, housing and other programs.

Shays, in a telephone news conference, said there may be some success in bringing Republican leaders around to the new technique once it is explained to them how open to manipulation the head-by-head count could be.
